newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh minister says budget protects industry.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh minister says budget protects industry.

text.p: Bangladesh's Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said on Saturday fiscal measures proposed in the 1997/98 budget would protect local industries.

"New fiscal measures were aimed at giving a breathing space to domestic industry. We wanted to give the industries a chance to survive," he told a post-budget dialogue organised by the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), a think tank.
Kibria announced the 1997/98 (July-June) budget in parliament on Thursday.

"They (local industries) were abruptly pushed to severe competition. Trade liberalisation went too fast in recent years. We liberalised faster than India, even faster than many South East Asian countries," the minister said.
"We don't want to push them further to harsher situation."
The new budget will make imports of finished products expensive by imposing higher duties, luxury taxes and import surcharge.
Duties on raw materials for local industries have been reduced and duty exemptions on many items lifted.
"(Import) liberalisation will be very much on our agenda in future, but we will not do it across the board," Kibria said.
Bangladesh, as part of an ambitious liberalisation programme, brought down its highest rate of import duty from 350 percent in 1991/92 to 45 percent in 1996/97.
The number of import banned items was reduced to 24 from 451 during the period.
Leading trade bodies claim that the massive trade liberalisation left more than 5,000 local industries either sick and dead.
Business leaders and economists said trade liberalisation failed to raise competitiveness of local industries in absence of matching reforms in other sectors of economy.
"Liberalisation should have simultaneously addressed other structural difficulties," said Debapriya Bhattachariya, reasearch fellow of the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies.
The brake in import liberalisation, however, drew fire from the World Bank, the agency guiding Bangladesh's trade reform under various policy-based commodity loans.
World Bank's Mission chief in Dhaka, Pierre Landell-Mills, said consumers had been burdened on the pretext of protecting the sick industries.

"I disagree with the Finance Minister that trade liberalisation (in Bangladesh) was very fast. There has been overwhelming evidence worldwide that liberalisation is good for the economy," Landell-Mills said.
He cautioned the government was risking to waste scarce resources by protecting inefficient industries.
Former Finance Minister A.M.A. Muhit also critcised duty rises, saying the policy was contradictory to the government's commitment to establish free trade area in South Asia by the year 2002.
"The signal looks unclear. The government should have clearly told the industries that there will be no protection in 2002."
